title: Dysphagia: Oropharyngeal or Esophageal Before You Choose the Test
bottomLine: Dysphagia is localized before it is investigated. Difficulty initiating a swallow, coughing/choking and aspiration clues suggest oropharyngeal disease; food sticking after swallowing suggests esophageal disease. Progressive solid-to-liquid dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding or inability to handle secretions requires urgent structural evaluation.
recognize: Oropharyngeal dysphagia often causes coughing, wet voice, nasal regurgitation or aspiration.
Esophageal dysphagia can reflect mechanical obstruction or motility disease; solids-only progressing to liquids is particularly concerning for obstruction.
differentiate: Odynophagia is painful swallowing and has a different infectious/inflammatory differential.
Globus without true swallowing impairment is not equivalent to dysphagia.
assessment: Assess onset/progression, solids vs liquids, aspiration/coughing, weight loss, reflux, neurologic disease, stroke history, medication/pill injury and cancer risk.
workup: Use swallow assessment/modified barium or speech-language evaluation for oropharyngeal patterns and endoscopy/barium/manometry pathways for esophageal disease according to the suspected mechanism.
Do not treat progressive dysphagia indefinitely as GERD without structural evaluation.
management: Protect aspiration risk, modify diet/feeding only with appropriate swallowing guidance and treat the identified structural, inflammatory or motility cause.
Food-bolus obstruction with inability to handle secretions requires emergency endoscopic care.
medicationSafety: Review pills that can injure the esophagus and sedatives that worsen aspiration risk.
Do not crush extended-release/enteric-coated medications indiscriminately when swallowing is impaired.
counselling: Teach safe swallowing strategies only after the mechanism is assessed and give aspiration/obstruction return precautions.
followUp: Close the loop on endoscopy/swallow studies and nutritional impact; persistent unexplained dysphagia requires specialty evaluation.
examTrap: Escalating a PPI for progressive dysphagia instead of localizing the swallowing problem and evaluating obstruction.
oneLinePearl: First ask where the swallow fails; then choose the test.

title: Anorectal Symptoms: Don't Call Every Rectal Bleed Hemorrhoids
bottomLine: Hemorrhoids, fissures, abscesses, fistulas, prolapse and neoplasia can present with anorectal symptoms. A visible hemorrhoid does not explain every episode of rectal bleeding; age/risk, anemia, bowel-pattern change and exam findings determine whether colorectal evaluation is still required.
recognize: Internal hemorrhoids commonly cause painless bright-red bleeding; fissures often cause sharp pain with defecation.
Perianal abscess causes focal pain/swelling and can progress to systemic infection.
differentiate: IBD, colorectal cancer, proctitis and diverticular/other bleeding can coexist with hemorrhoids.
Thrombosed external hemorrhoid and abscess are different painful perianal conditions with different treatment.
assessment: Assess bleeding amount/pattern, pain, bowel habits, constipation/straining, pregnancy, anticoagulants, anemia/weight loss, IBD risk and colorectal screening status.
workup: Perform appropriate inspection/digital/anoscopy when indicated and use colon evaluation based on age/risk/alarm features rather than assuming the anorectal finding is the whole diagnosis.
management: Use fibre/stool-softening/behaviour measures and topical/procedural treatment matched to the anorectal diagnosis.
Drain abscess urgently and refer complex fistula/prolapse/refractory hemorrhoidal disease.
medicationSafety: Avoid prolonged topical steroid use without reassessment.
Anticoagulated bleeding requires source/severity assessment rather than automatic cessation without thrombosis-risk review.
counselling: Teach stool consistency/straining prevention and explain why bleeding may still need colon evaluation despite known hemorrhoids.
followUp: Reassess persistent symptoms and ensure colorectal workup is completed when indicated.
examTrap: Attributing iron-deficiency anemia and rectal bleeding to hemorrhoids without investigating the colon.
oneLinePearl: Hemorrhoids can bleed; they do not cancel the colorectal differential.

title: Abdominal Pain: Decide Who Is Unsafe Before Naming the Diagnosis
bottomLine: Abdominal pain is a disposition problem before it is a final-diagnosis problem. Identify shock, peritonitis, pregnancy emergencies, obstruction, ischemia, perforation, bleeding and other time-sensitive disease first, then use location/tempo/associated symptoms and targeted tests to narrow the cause.
recognize: Pain out of proportion, rigid abdomen, involuntary guarding, shock, GI bleeding, persistent vomiting and toxic appearance are dangerous clues.
Older/immunocompromised patients can have muted tenderness/fever despite serious disease.
differentiate: Cardiac, pulmonary, metabolic, vascular, gynecologic and genitourinary disease can present as abdominal pain.
Pain severity alone does not identify surgical disease; physiology and exam pattern matter.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, onset/location/migration, vomiting/stool/urine, bleeding, fever, prior surgery, medications/anticoagulants and pregnancy possibility.
Perform focused abdominal and relevant pelvic/testicular/cardiopulmonary exam.
workup: Use CBC/chemistry/liver/pancreatic/urine/pregnancy/ECG or imaging according to the differential; choose ultrasound when it answers biliary/pelvic/pregnancy questions without unnecessary radiation.
management: Provide analgesia/antiemetics while evaluating and escalate peritonitis, ischemia, perforation, obstructed infected systems, ectopic pregnancy and instability.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs can worsen GI bleeding/renal disease; opioids require monitoring but should not be withheld from severe pain solely for fear of masking diagnosis.
counselling: For appropriate outpatient care, give explicit return precautions for worsening pain, fever, vomiting, bleeding, syncope or inability to hydrate.
followUp: Own pending imaging/lab results and reassess unresolved pain rather than accepting a nonspecific diagnosis indefinitely.
examTrap: Delaying analgesia or emergency referral while trying to force a final diagnosis in a patient with peritonitis or shock.
oneLinePearl: In abdominal pain, disposition comes before diagnostic perfection.
sourceBasis: Canadian emergency/primary-care abdominal pain practice principles

title: Liver Tests in GI Disease: Injury, Cholestasis, and Synthetic Function Are Different Axes
bottomLine: AST/ALT primarily reflect hepatocellular injury, alkaline phosphatase/bilirubin help define cholestatic patterns, and INR/albumin contribute information about synthetic function in the appropriate context. Do not call aminotransferase elevation 'liver failure' or assume falling AST/ALT means recovery when INR, bilirubin or mental status worsen.
recognize: Hepatocellular and cholestatic patterns narrow the differential more than an isolated value.
ALP can arise from bone/placenta and AST from muscle, so source/context matter.
differentiate: Albumin changes slowly and is influenced by inflammation/nutrition/renal loss; it is not a rapid acute-liver-failure marker.
Normal/mild AST/ALT does not exclude advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis.
assessment: Assess jaundice, pruritus, pain, hemodynamics, alcohol/medications/supplements, pregnancy, viral/metabolic risk and encephalopathy/bleeding.
workup: Classify the biochemical pattern, then use cause-directed viral/metabolic/autoimmune/toxicologic tests and ultrasound/other imaging.
Assess INR/glucose/mental status in significant acute injury rather than trending enzymes alone.
management: Treat the cause and escalate acute liver failure, cholangitis/obstruction or severe deterioration urgently.
Stable chronic abnormalities require fibrosis/etiology assessment rather than indefinite repeat panels.
medicationSafety: Review hepatotoxic drugs based on pattern/severity and avoid blanket discontinuation from one mild isolated enzyme rise.
counselling: Explain that 'liver function tests' contain markers with different jobs and should be read as a pattern.
followUp: Trend the abnormalities that answer the clinical question and close the loop on definitive etiologic/fibrosis workup.
examTrap: Declaring liver recovery because AST/ALT fall while INR and mental status worsen.
oneLinePearl: Read liver tests by job: injury, bile flow and synthetic function.

title: GI Tumor Markers: Monitor Selected Known Disease, Don't Screen the Population
bottomLine: CEA, CA 19-9, AFP and other tumor markers are context-dependent adjuncts. Most are not sufficiently specific or sensitive for population cancer screening or stand-alone diagnosis; use them only when a defined known/suspected cancer pathway gives the result a meaningful role.
recognize: Tumor markers can rise from benign inflammation, biliary obstruction, smoking or other conditions.
Trends can support response/recurrence monitoring in selected diagnosed cancers when baseline marker biology is relevant.
differentiate: A high marker is not a cancer diagnosis; a normal marker does not exclude cancer.
AFP use in HCC-risk pathways differs from using it as a general abdominal-cancer screen.
assessment: Clarify the specific suspected/known malignancy, prior treatment, imaging/pathology and why the marker is being ordered.
workup: Use imaging/endoscopy/pathology as the diagnostic foundation and order tumor markers only according to the disease-specific pathway.
management: Act on marker trends only in conjunction with the clinical/imaging context and oncology/hepatology plan.
Do not chase isolated mild elevations with repeated panels absent a clinical indication.
medicationSafety: Avoid delaying diagnostic imaging/biopsy because a tumor marker is normal.
Do not expose patients to unnecessary invasive testing based solely on a nonspecific elevation.
redFlags: Cancer alarm symptoms with falsely reassuring marker
Rapid marker rise in known disease
counselling: Explain that tumor markers are clues/monitoring tools, not yes/no cancer tests.
followUp: Track only markers that are useful for the specific disease and coordinate interpretation with the responsible specialty team.
examTrap: Ordering CEA or CA 19-9 as population screening tests—or ruling out cancer because the marker is normal.
oneLinePearl: Tumor markers support a cancer pathway; they do not create one.

title: Endoscopy: Scope When the Answer Changes Management
bottomLine: Endoscopy is appropriate when it can diagnose, risk-stratify or treat a clinically meaningful GI problem. Alarm dysphagia, bleeding, anemia, positive screening, high-risk surveillance and persistent/refractory disease are common indications; routine repeat procedures without a decision attached add burden and risk.
recognize: Urgent endoscopy may be needed for significant GI bleeding, food bolus obstruction or selected biliary/other emergencies.
Elective endoscopy is used for alarm symptoms, diagnostic uncertainty and evidence-based surveillance.
differentiate: Screening/surveillance procedures differ from symptom-driven diagnostic procedures.
Not every uncomplicated reflux/dyspepsia/IBS symptom needs endoscopy.
assessment: Define the clinical question, urgency, bleeding/thrombotic risk, sedation/airway risk, comorbidity and whether the patient can complete preparation/follow-up.
workup: Choose upper/lower endoscopy, ERCP/EUS or alternate imaging based on the suspected disease and whether therapeutic intervention is needed.
management: Use pathology/procedure findings to create an explicit treatment/surveillance plan and ensure urgent findings are closed-loop communicated.
Avoid ERCP as purely diagnostic when safer noninvasive imaging can answer the question.
medicationSafety: Antithrombotic/diabetes medication management is procedure- and risk-specific; use current endoscopy guidance rather than universal holds.
Sedation planning must account for OSA, frailty and respiratory/cardiac risk.
counselling: Explain why the procedure is being done, what result would change care and what post-procedure symptoms require urgent review.
followUp: Own pathology/results and the next surveillance/referral interval; the procedure is not complete until results are acted on.
examTrap: Ordering routine repeat endoscopy with no new alarm/risk indication or follow-up question.
oneLinePearl: Every scope should answer a clinical question and produce a follow-up plan.

title: Nutrition Assessment: Treat Deficiency and Intake Barriers, Not a Lab Panel
bottomLine: Nutrition assessment integrates weight trajectory, intake, function, swallowing/GI symptoms, disease burden and social access. Supplements should correct a demonstrated or highly plausible need; broad micronutrient panels and indiscriminate supplementation can miss the real problem or create toxicity.
recognize: Unintentional weight loss, reduced intake, muscle loss, functional decline and recurrent deficiency raise nutrition risk.
Obesity does not exclude malnutrition or micronutrient deficiency.
differentiate: Inflammation can alter albumin/prealbumin and they are not stand-alone nutrition-status tests.
Weight loss from malignancy/endocrine/psychiatric disease needs diagnosis, not only calorie supplements.
assessment: Assess recent weight/intake, food insecurity, swallowing/dentition, GI loss/malabsorption, medications, pregnancy, alcohol and functional ability to shop/cook/eat.
workup: Use cause-directed CBC/iron/B12/folate/electrolyte/vitamin tests when risk or symptoms justify them rather than shotgun panels.
Assess refeeding risk in severe malnutrition before aggressive nutrition restoration.
management: Treat the cause, optimize oral intake and use dietitian support/oral/enteral/parenteral supplementation according to gut function and severity.
Address food access and disability barriers as part of treatment.
medicationSafety: Excess fat-soluble vitamins/minerals can cause toxicity and interact with medications.
Refeeding requires phosphate/magnesium/potassium/thiamine awareness in high-risk patients.
counselling: Focus on function, strength and adequate intake rather than moralizing food or weight.
followUp: Track weight trajectory, function, intake and the specific deficiency/goal being treated.
examTrap: Diagnosing malnutrition from low albumin alone or prescribing multiple supplements without identifying why intake/absorption is failing.
oneLinePearl: Nutrition is a clinical assessment with targeted labs—not a supplement shopping list.

title: Short Bowel Syndrome: Manage Fluid, Electrolytes, Nutrition, and Adaptation Together
bottomLine: Short bowel syndrome is intestinal failure physiology: reduced absorptive surface causes fluid/electrolyte loss, nutrient deficiency and sometimes parenteral-support dependence. Management must be individualized to remaining anatomy, output and adaptation—not reduced to 'treat diarrhea.'
recognize: High-output stool/stoma, dehydration, magnesium/sodium loss, weight loss and micronutrient deficiency are common.
Colon continuity and remaining small-bowel segments strongly influence fluid and nutrient management.
differentiate: High-output stoma/SBS differs from infectious diarrhea and may worsen with inappropriate hypotonic fluid intake.
Bile-acid diarrhea, bacterial overgrowth and pancreatic/other malabsorption can contribute differently.
assessment: Assess surgical anatomy, stool/stoma output, urine output, thirst, weight, medications, oral intake, renal function, electrolytes and parenteral/enteral support.
workup: Trend renal/electrolyte/magnesium/nutrition markers and cause-directed vitamin/mineral levels; quantify output and hydration rather than relying on symptoms alone.
management: Use specialized intestinal-rehabilitation care with oral rehydration composition, diet, antimotility/acid suppression and enteral/parenteral support tailored to anatomy/output.
Aim to reduce dehydration and parenteral needs as adaptation permits while preventing malnutrition.
medicationSafety: Drug absorption may be reduced; extended-release formulations and medications requiring specific intestinal sites may be unreliable.
Antimotility/antisecretory dosing is specialist-guided and renal/electrolyte effects require monitoring.
redFlags: Progressive liver disease on parenteral nutrition
counselling: Teach individualized oral rehydration, output/urine monitoring and when high output requires urgent contact.
followUp: Coordinate intestinal-rehabilitation/nutrition care and track renal function, growth/weight, micronutrients, line complications and support requirements.
examTrap: Telling a patient with high-output short bowel to drink unlimited plain water without considering sodium/glucose-coupled absorption and output.
oneLinePearl: Short bowel management is anatomy plus hydration plus nutrition—not diarrhea suppression alone.
